CausalChain: Chronic liver injury → activation of CAFs → secretion of CXCL11 → recruitment of pro-tumor T cell subsets that enhance CSC renewal → metabolic reprogramming in HCC elevates SAM/MTA → epigenetic modifications leading to increased immune checkpoint expression (PD-1/CTLA-4) → T cell exhaustion and impaired anti-tumor response
Hypothesis: In HCC, we hypothesize that precise inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase will attenuate the production of SAM/MTA and thereby disrupt the epigenetic upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules that drive T cell exhaustion. Concurrent blockade of the CXCL11/CXCR3 axis using targeted biologics or small molecules will prevent the recruitment of T cell subsets that support CSC renewal. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene editing, single-cell transcriptomics, and computational pathway modeling, we aim to validate the mechanistic links in this dual-target strategy. This combined therapeutic intervention is expected to restore robust anti-tumor immunity, diminish CSC maintenance, and ultimately reduce tumor progression in HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often arises from a chronically injured liver, where activated cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) secrete chemokines such as CXCL11, recruiting T cell subsets that paradoxically support cancer stem cell (CSC) renewal. Concurrently, metabolic reprogramming in HCC elevates S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA), driving epigenetic changes that upregulate immune checkpoint molecules (PD-1, CTLA-4) and culminate in T cell exhaustion. We propose a dual intervention that leverages state-of-the-art molecular tools and single-cell technologies to inhibit methionine adenosyltransferase, thereby reducing SAM/MTA-mediated epigenetic reprogramming, and simultaneously block the CXCL11/CXCR3 axis to prevent recruitment of T cell subsets that sustain CSC properties. This integrative approach is designed to synergistically rejuvenate anti-tumor immunity, overcome immune suppression, and slow tumor progression in HCC, with mechanistic validation through CRISPR-Cas9 screening, high-dimensional single-cell RNA sequencing, and computational modeling.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase and blockade of the CXCL11/CXCR3 axis would synergistically restore anti-tumor immunity in HCC by reducing T cell exhaustion and CSC renewal. The revised hypothesis retains these core elements but explicitly incorporates advanced technological capabilities such as single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR screening to dissect and validate the mechanistic causal chain. Each step—starting from chronic liver injury and CAF activation, moving to chemokine secretion and pro-tumor T cell recruitment, then to metabolic reprogramming with SAM/MTA elevation and epigenetic checkpoint upregulation, ending in T cell exhaustion—is systematically addressed. This not only refines the mechanistic rationale but also improves practical implementability by proposing precise and state-of-the-art methods for intervention and validation.
